It was developed to address the limitations of MPVO, which only computes an approximate ordering for general (non-convex) datasets, resulting in visual artifacts [S1][S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the method (implied to be the one being discussed or the MPVONC heuristic itself, depending on context, but the evidence supports the description of MPVONC's limitations) was developed to address limitations of MPVO, specifically that MPVO only computes an approximate ordering for general (non-convex) datasets, resulting in visual artifacts. Source [S2] explicitly states: '...this method [MPVO] only computes an approximate ordering in general datasets, resulting in visual artifacts when rendered.' It also mentions that MPVONC was developed to extend MPVO to nonconvex meshes. The evidence confirms that MPVO's limitation is its approximate nature on non-convex/general data leading to artifacts, and MPVONC was the heuristic developed to handle non-convex meshes (though it also has limitations). The claim accurately reflects the content of the sources regarding MPVO's limitations and the context of MPVONC's development.

Unlike exact methods such as [Exact Visibility Ordering for Cell Projection Volume Rendering (SXMPVO)](944-exact-visibility-ordering-for-cell-projection-volume-renderi.md) or [A-buffer visibility sort for non-convex grids](1057-a-buffer-visibility-sort-for-non-convex-grids.md), MPVONC is significantly faster but is approximate; it may produce visual artifacts due to sorting errors when occlusion relationships are not captured by the topological graph [S1][S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The evidence supports all components of the claim. The sources explicitly state that MPVONC is a heuristic extension of MPVO that is 'very fast' (supporting 'significantly faster' compared to exact methods mentioned in S2 as 'previous exact methods'). The sources also confirm that MPVONC is approximate and can fail, leading to 'visual artifacts from sorting errors' (S1, S2, S3). Specifically, S1, S2, and S3 detail that these errors occur when occlusion relationships are not captured by the topological graph (specifically across ray-gaps where centroid distance sorting fails), which aligns with the claim's explanation of why artifacts occur.
